Getting started with dar

Source: vignettes/dar.Rmd
dar.Rmd

dar provides a common interface for configuring, running and comparing differential abundance methods. A recipe records preprocessing steps, a shared statistical design and the methods to execute. The prepared recipe contains per-method results; consensus is an optional summary, not a required endpoint.

Example data

The included metaHIV_phy object is a phyloseq dataset from Noguera-Julian et al. (2016). Here we compare its recorded RiskGroup2 categories. This unadjusted example illustrates the software; it does not establish causal effects or validated microbial biomarkers.

data("metaHIV_phy", package = "dar")
metaHIV_phy
#> phyloseq-class experiment-level object
#> otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 451 taxa and 156 samples ]
#> sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 156 samples by 3 sample variables ]
#> tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 451 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]

Configure a workflow

Create a recipe and define the model once with add_model(). targets selects the variable whose effects are tested; other fixed terms can adjust for covariates. tax_level selects the rank at which methods analyze the data. An explicit reference makes the direction of comparisons clear.

rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy) |>
  add_model(
    ~ RiskGroup2,
    targets = "RiskGroup2",
    tax_level = "Species",
    reference = c(RiskGroup2 = "hts")
  ) |>
  step_subset_taxa(tax_level = "Kingdom", taxa = c("Bacteria", "Archaea")) |>
  step_filter_by_prevalence(threshold = 0.03) |>
  step_deseq(id = "deseq") |>
  step_maaslin(min_prevalence = 0, id = "maaslin")

rec
#> ── DAR Recipe ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>      ℹ phyloseq object with 451 taxa and 156 samples 
#>      ℹ variable of interes RiskGroup2 (class: character, levels: hts, msm, pwid) 
#>      ℹ taxonomic level Species 
#> 
#> Statistical model:
#> 
#>      ℹ ~RiskGroup2 
#> 
#> Preprocessing steps:
#> 
#>      ◉ step_subset_taxa() id = subset_taxa__Ensaïmada 
#>      ◉ step_filter_by_prevalence() id = filter_by_prevalence__Puff_pastry 
#> 
#> DA steps:
#> 
#>      ◉ step_deseq() id = deseq 
#>      ◉ step_maaslin() id = maaslin

The prevalence step retains taxa present in more than 3% of samples. We disable MaAsLin3’s additional prevalence filter because the recipe already defines a shared filter; this does not make the engines’ assumptions or effect scales identical. These two compatible methods illustrate the interface, not a universally recommended panel.

Run the recipe

prep() applies preprocessing in order, resolves the shared model and runs compatible methods. This guide uses sequential execution. For separate worker processes, use parallel = TRUE and choose workers for the available memory.

fit <- prep(rec, parallel = FALSE)
fit
#> ── DAR Results ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>      ℹ phyloseq object with 278 taxa and 156 samples 
#>      ℹ variable of interes RiskGroup2 (class: character, levels: hts, msm, pwid) 
#>      ℹ taxonomic level Species 
#> 
#> Results:
#> 
#>      ✔ deseq diff_taxa = 155 
#>      ✔ maaslin diff_taxa = 47 
#> 
#>      ℹ 35 taxon-contrast effects are present in all tested methods

Inspect per-method results

tidy_results() returns a common table with taxon IDs, contrasts, effect scales, statistics and method decisions. method identifies the engine and step_id identifies its configured instance. Native effect scales remain distinct; uniform columns do not imply interchangeable effect sizes or p-values.

results <- tidy_results(fit)
results |>
  dplyr::select(
    taxa_id, contrast_id, effect_size, effect_metric,
    adj_p_value, significant, method, step_id
  ) |>
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   taxa_id contrast_id   effect_size effect_metric adj_p_value significant method
#>   <chr>   <chr>               <dbl> <chr>               <dbl> <lgl>       <chr> 
#> 1 Otu_1   RiskGroup2[m…       0.640 log2_fold_ch…    4.70e- 1 FALSE       deseq 
#> 2 Otu_2   RiskGroup2[m…       1.58  log2_fold_ch…    2.10e- 1 FALSE       deseq 
#> 3 Otu_7   RiskGroup2[m…       1.28  log2_fold_ch…    3.53e- 1 FALSE       deseq 
#> 4 Otu_10  RiskGroup2[m…       1.39  log2_fold_ch…    9.84e- 2 FALSE       deseq 
#> 5 Otu_11  RiskGroup2[m…      23.3   log2_fold_ch…    4.46e-12 TRUE        deseq 
#> 6 Otu_12  RiskGroup2[m…       2.23  log2_fold_ch…    9.35e- 2 FALSE       deseq 
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: step_id <chr>

results |>
  dplyr::group_by(step_id, contrast_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_significant = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   step_id contrast_id          n_significant
#>   <chr>   <chr>                        <int>
#> 1 deseq   RiskGroup2[msm-hts]            121
#> 2 deseq   RiskGroup2[pwid-hts]            63
#> 3 deseq   RiskGroup2[pwid-msm]           108
#> 4 maaslin RiskGroup2[msm-hts]             39
#> 5 maaslin RiskGroup2[pwid-hts]             5
#> 6 maaslin RiskGroup2[pwid-msm]            21

These results can be used directly, without bake() or cool().

Plot a selected comparison

Plots accept explicit contrast selectors so distinct hypotheses are not mixed. Here we show up to six taxa detected by at least one method for the comparison of msm with hts. An empty selection is a valid result, not a plotting failure.

comparison_id <- "RiskGroup2[msm-hts]"
taxa_ids <- results |>
  dplyr::filter(contrast_id == comparison_id, significant) |>
  dplyr::distinct(taxa_id) |>
  dplyr::pull(taxa_id) |>
  head(6)

if (length(taxa_ids)) {
  abundance_plt(
    fit, taxa_ids = taxa_ids,
    contrast_id = comparison_id, type = "boxplot"
  )
} else {
  message("No significant taxa for this comparison.")
}
#> You have inserted a phyloseq object. The phyloseq-based methods will be deprecated. We recommend switching to the (Tree)SummarizedExperiment framework and mia R/Bioconductor package.
